scenes.text: Your toilet doesn't push the water out. It sucks it out. Let's cut it open. Hidden in the base is a bent pipe called the trapway. It climbs, then drops to the drain. The water in the bowl can only sit as high as the top of that bend. Add more, and it spills over. That's why the level never changes. That water also blocks sewer gas. Now press the handle. A chain lifts a rubber flap called the flapper, and the tank dumps in at once. It rushes through holes under the rim, and a jet near the bottom. The bend fills up completely, and that's the trick. Water falling down the drain pulls the bowl after it. That's a siphon. It keeps pulling until air gets into the pipe. That's the gurgle at the end. Then the flapper drops and seals the tank. A float falls with the water and opens the fill valve. A small tube refills the bowl, so the seal comes back. As the float rises, it shuts the water off. If it ever fails, the overflow tube sends extra water into the bowl, not onto your floor. In the US, a new toilet can use at most one point six gallons per flush. Have you ever had to flush with a bucket? Tell me in the comments. Next up: how they build a dam across a river. Follow so you don't miss it.
